newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn parliament urges international cloning ban.
newsitem.headline: Bonn parliament urges international cloning ban.

text.p: The German parliament on Friday called on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to campaign for a comprehensive international ban on the cloning of human beings.

The parliament, alarmed by the recent cloning of a sheep in Britain which has revived memories here of Nazi tampering with science, also asked the government to make sure German laws offered no possibility for human cloning.
Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers assured deputies that cloning humans was already banned in Germany, and vowed Bonn would fight for similarly tough regulations across the world.
"The cloning of human beings is forbidden in Germany and there is no research going on in Germany with the aim of cloning human beings," he told parliament.

Parliament's resolution, which was passed unanimously, also stressed that any attempt to clone human beings would be against Germany's constitution. Article One states that "the dignity of man shall be inviolable".

The announcement by scientists at the Roslin Institue in eastern Scotland last month that they had cloned an adult sheep touched a raw nerve in Germany, where memories of Nazi plans for a blue-eyed, blond-haired master race remain sensitive.

Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig said his ministry was permanently checking laws to make sure they were not outdated. It was natural Germany should have particularly strict rules on genetic engineering because of its past, he added.

"Anyone who clones a person makes that person into an object," Schmidt-Jortzig told parliament. "A society in which people create other people according to their wishes is no longer based on the foundations of human civilisation."
The Nazis adopted the "science" of eugenics in their drive to breed an Aryan master race.

According to the doctrine, some people were fit to live and breed while others, such as the mentally and physically handicapped, were deemed genetically inferior, and had to be destroyed or at least sterilised.
Ruettgers said some of the arguments he had heard in favour of human cloning -- such as providing donors for transplants -- reminded him of the theories of "Nazi barbarism".
"It can never be the case that we breed people in order to then cut them up," he said, to applause from deputies.

Some members of parliament criticised the government for its contribution to a recent Council of Europe convention on biomedicine, saying its regulations on research were more lax than Germany's strict domestic laws.
But the ministers said the agreement, although not ideal, was better than none at all.
"This convention only sets minimum standards," Schmidt-Jortzig said. "We are not prevented at all from continuing to work to uphold our own higher standards."
